title: Can AI Really Buy Things for You? What AI Shopping Actually Does in 2026
summary: AI is now a mainstream shopping research tool, but fully autonomous checkout largely stalled. Here's what actually works today and what to watch for.
before: AI will handle your entire shopping journey from discovery to checkout, all inside the chat window.
after: AI excels at research and narrowing choices, but you still complete the purchase yourself on the merchant's site.
body:
If you have tried asking ChatGPT or Perplexity to help you find a new laptop or a pair of running shoes, you have experienced the current reality of AI shopping. It is genuinely useful for research. But the promise that AI would buy things for you, handling everything from discovery to payment inside a single conversation, has largely not materialized. Here is what actually works, what stalled, and what you should watch for as a shopper.

## AI as a Research Assistant: This Part Works

Using AI for product research has gone mainstream. According to Alchemer's 2026 Retail Report, <cite index="43-1,43-5">48.5% of shoppers used an AI tool to research a purchase in the past year, with tools like ChatGPT and Claude closing in on social media and review sites as research channels.</cite>

When you describe what you need in plain language, AI assistants can pull together product options, compare features, and explain trade-offs. <cite index="17-8,17-9">In AI Mode, shoppers ask longer, more specific questions than they do in keyword search. Instead of typing "blue running shoes," someone might ask: "What's the best running shoe for wide feet on hot pavement, under $150?"</cite> This is where AI genuinely saves time.

<cite index="41-1">Consumers are currently most comfortable using AI help for price comparison (55%) and package tracking (47%).</cite> These are straightforward tasks that do not require much judgment. The pattern is clear: AI works well as a research concierge, less well as an autonomous buyer.

## Why In-Chat Checkout Stalled

In September 2025, OpenAI launched Instant Checkout inside ChatGPT with significant fanfare. <cite index="7-1,7-2">OpenAI retired Instant Checkout in March 2026, about six months after it launched, and repositioned ChatGPT toward product discovery, with checkout moving back to merchants' own environments.</cite>

What went wrong? <cite index="10-8,10-9">According to Forrester principal analyst Emily Pfeiffer, only about 30 Shopify merchants had participated in Instant Checkout as of February 2026. Walmart offered approximately 200,000 products, but the onboarding process was cumbersome, and inventory, shipping cost, and other information was frequently inaccurate.</cite> The fundamental problem was data quality: <cite index="10-10,10-11">OpenAI was scraping retail sites to obtain product information, making it impossible to accurately reflect real-time inventory and pricing data.</cite>

<cite index="11-5">Walmart measured checkout inside ChatGPT converting roughly 3x worse than a click-through to Walmart, even as ChatGPT drove about 2x the new-customer rate of search.</cite> In other words, AI was great at bringing in new shoppers, but they still wanted to complete their purchase on the merchant's familiar checkout page.

## What the Major Platforms Offer Now

**ChatGPT** has shifted to a discovery-first model. <cite index="2-5">In place of checkout, ChatGPT is getting richer visual shopping tools, including side-by-side product comparisons, image-based search for finding similar items, and conversational result filtering.</cite> <cite index="4-9">As of 2026, the shopping feature shows no advertising and no paid placement; products appear based on relevance to your request.</cite>

**Google** is pushing harder on agentic checkout through its Universal Commerce Protocol. <cite index="18-11">These experiences include conversational product discovery, virtual try-on, and emerging features like agentic checkout, where AI can complete checkout steps on a shopper's behalf with prior consent.</cite> <cite index="20-2">Shoppers will soon be able to browse product listings and buy directly from Target in AI Mode in Google Search and the Gemini app.</cite>

**Perplexity** offers Instant Buy. <cite index="25-10,25-11">Perplexity's in-chat purchase option is Instant Buy, a new feature built with PayPal as the payment method. Shoppers can complete a purchase from participating retailers without leaving Perplexity.</cite> <cite index="31-1,31-2">In 2026, Perplexity officially discontinued advertising and is targeting $500 million in annualized revenue entirely from subscriptions. This removes the conflict of interest between sponsored placements and organic recommendations.</cite>

**Anthropic** just released open-source blueprints for merchants to build their own shopping agents. <cite index="35-7">Anthropic says customers already using Claude-based shopping agents have seen shopping carts grow by as much as 35% and shoppers become 60% more likely to complete a purchase.</cite> But notably, <cite index="37-6">shopping agents can make preference-based suggestions and add items to a customer's cart, but they do not complete purchases.</cite>

## Consumers Want Help, Not Autopilot

The most important data point for understanding AI shopping in 2026 is this: <cite index="51-7">consumer willingness to let AI make purchase decisions topped out at 11% across lower-stakes categories, such as personal care and household supplies, according to Gartner.</cite>

<cite index="51-2,51-3">"Consumers are not looking to outsource shopping decisions to AI," said Kate Muhl, VP Analyst in the Gartner Marketing practice. "They want AI to help them find better information, compare prices, identify deals and narrow choices, while keeping final decision-making control for themselves."</cite>

<cite index="19-5">A ChannelEngine study of 4,500 shoppers found that only 17% feel comfortable letting AI complete a purchase, even as many consumers already use AI to research products.</cite>

## What to Watch For as a Shopper

**Verify AI claims.** <cite index="47-2">Among shoppers who used AI for product research in the past 90 days, 86% verified the AI's recommendation through another source before buying.</cite> That is a reasonable approach. AI can surface options, but double-check prices and availability on the merchant's site.

**Watch for paid relationships.** Currently, major AI shopping platforms claim their results are organic and not paid. <cite index="25-8">Perplexity has confirmed that results are organic; brands can't pay for placement.</cite> This could change, so stay alert for disclosure notices.

**Set your own limits.** If you do use features that allow AI to add items to a cart or complete purchases, make sure you understand what spending limits and approval steps exist. <cite index="46-1">Trust remains a barrier to adoption with 27% of consumers saying they trust no organization to operate an AI shopping agent, and 24% saying they will never delegate purchases to AI.</cite>

The bottom line: AI has become a genuinely useful shopping research tool. But the vision of fully autonomous agents buying things on your behalf is still early, limited by both technical challenges and simple consumer preference. For now, the model that works is "discover in AI, buy on the merchant's site." That is not a failure. It is how most people actually want to shop.
